This page makes the case for the measurement method `system_ident` implements — an
**optimal-excitation, periodic-multisine, frequency-domain** identification in the
[Pintelon–Schoukens](overview.qmd) ("P&S") tradition — and weighs it fairly against the two
excitations most subsystems reach for first: **broadband random noise** and the **swept
sine**. It is written for engineers in *any* LIGO subsystem — suspensions, seismic/ISI,
DARM/calibration, ALS, OMC — because the argument is about the measurement, not the plant.

The thesis is not "multisine always wins." It is: **when measurement time is expensive,
drive is bounded, the plant is high-Q, and the loop is closed, optimal-excitation ID buys you
more parameter precision per second and per count of drive than the alternatives — and we can
show it, not just assert it.** Where a swept sine or random noise is the right tool, this page
says so.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}

## 1 · The measurement problem, and the figures of merit

Every subsystem identification looks the same once you squint: a plant with **sharp, high-Q
resonances** packed into a **narrow band**, observed through a **noisy readout**, driven by an
actuator with a **hard amplitude limit**, often **inside a closed loop** — and you get only so
much **observing time** to measure it before the instrument must go back to work.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "A representative suspension plant over its readout floor"
md.problem_fig()
```

So a method is good or bad only relative to what you actually pay and get. We score every
excitation on the same five figures of merit:

- **Parameter / FRF uncertainty per unit time** — the Cramér–Rao σ (or σ/θ) reached for a
  given total measurement time. *Less time for the same σ is the prize.*
- **Uncertainty per unit in-band drive power** — the same σ for a given **RMS** (in-band power)
  budget. Drive is ultimately capped by actuator saturation, so this is a hard currency too. We
  report RMS **plant-referred**; the *peak* that truly binds is set at the DAC, after the
  whitening/actuation chain this simulation does not model (see §2.1 and §9).
- **Leakage bias** — does the estimator read a sharp resonance at its true height, or smear it?
  A bias no amount of averaging removes.
- **Per-bin noise model** — does the method *measure* its own error bar on each frequency, or
  must you assume one?
- **Safety** — whether the method is safe to run **closed-loop**, and how much in-band drive
  power it asks of the actuator.

The rest of this page is those five columns, filled with real numbers.

## 2 · The three excitations, fairly

All three put energy into the plant and watch it respond. They differ in *how the energy is
distributed in frequency and time* — and that difference is the whole story.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "The same in-band power as swept sine, random noise, and a multisine"
md.excitations_fig()
```

- **Swept sine** drives **one frequency at a time**, dwelling long enough to beat down noise at
  that line. It is leakage-free per line, trivially interpretable, and spends *all* its power
  where it is pointed — but it visits the band **serially**.
- **Broadband random noise** drives **every frequency at once** with random phase. It is the
  fastest way to a qualitative whole-band picture and an honest coherence — but it is **not
  periodic**, so its DFT leaks, and a single record gives no internal error bar.
- **Periodic multisine** also drives every frequency at once, with a period **exactly equal to
  the analysis window**, tiled and repeated. **That periodicity — not the choice of phase — is
  what makes the measurement leakage-free and self-error-barred**, and it is the substrate the
  optimal design shapes. The line *phases* are a free choice (the package defaults to Schroeder);
  as §2.1 shows, they do not affect the FRF or its error bar at all.

The crest factors printed above are real but **plant-referred** — peak/RMS of the digital
*request*, not of the waveform at the actuator's hard limit. Because crest factor is not
invariant under filtering, a low plant-referred crest does **not** imply a low crest at the DAC
once a whitening/actuation chain sits in between. This page therefore claims **no** crest- or
peak-drive advantage from phasing; §2.1 makes that case in full.

### 2.1 · Phasing: Schroeder vs random — a plant-referred fact, not a measurement advantage

A multisine's line *phases* are free: they set only the **time-domain crest factor** (peak/RMS)
of the drive, nothing else. It is worth being precise about what that does and does not buy,
because the textbook framing — "Schroeder phases minimise the crest factor, so a saturation-
limited actuator carries more power" — is true only in a reference frame this simulation cannot
actually reach.

**Schroeder really is lower-crest, in plant-referred units.** The package default
(`phase="schroeder"`) minimises peak/RMS of the *requested* waveform; random phasing does not.
The gap is real and grows with the number of lines:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Real crest factors: Schroeder vs random, vs number of lines (flat broadband)"
ph = md.phasing_crest_campaign()
md.phasing_crest_fig(ph)
```

Schroeder sits near a constant ≈1.9 regardless of line count; random phasing climbs as ≈√(ln N),
from comparable at a handful of lines to roughly **2× worse** across hundreds of flat lines. On
the **concentrated optimal ASD** this page actually drives with — a couple dozen significant
lines piled at the modes — the gap is **much smaller**:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Crest on the concentrated optimal ASD vs a flat one (printed inline)"
display(md.phasing_shape_md(ph))
```

So in plant-referred units Schroeder is lower-crest, but for the few concentrated lines the
optimal design uses the margin over random is modest (~1.4×), not the order-of-magnitude the
"hard actuator limit" framing implies.

**But phasing does not change the measurement at all.** The leakage-free FRF and its Cramér–Rao
bound depend on the line **amplitudes/power**, not the phases — the CRB function does not even
take phase as an argument. Driving the *same* plant with the *same* PSD and the *same* noise
seeds, Schroeder and random phasing recover statistically identical FRFs, identical per-bin σ,
and an identical CRB:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Phase-invariance of the estimate: Schroeder vs random, same plant/PSD/seeds"
pin = md.phasing_invariance_campaign()
display(md.phasing_invariance_table(pin))
```

**Why the crest advantage is moot here — the DAC reference frame.** In LIGO the actuator's hard
saturation limit lives at the **DAC** (counts/volts), and there are **whitening and actuation
filters between the digital excitation request and the DAC**. Crest factor is *not* invariant
under filtering: the whitening filter reshapes the waveform, scrambling the carefully optimised
Schroeder phases, so the DAC-frame crest is generally higher and unrelated to the plant-referred
crest minimised above. **Minimising crest in plant units therefore buys nothing at the DAC — the
limit that actually binds — and this simulation does not model the whitening chain, so it cannot
even represent the DAC frame.**

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## The honest bottom line on phasing
Phase touches **only** the crest factor, and crest is a **DAC-frame** quantity this plant-referred
simulation does not model. Since the estimate is phase-invariant (table above) and the one thing
phase affects does not transfer to the binding limit, **the phase choice is not load-bearing
here: random phases are essentially as good as Schroeder for our purposes.** A genuine crest /
peak-drive optimisation is a *DAC-frame, filter-aware* problem (push the optimisation through the
whitening chain) — future work, not a claim this page makes from plant-referred numbers.
:::

## 3 · Broadband random noise leaks, and is variance-inefficient

The case against random noise is not aesthetic. On a **high-Q resonance** — exactly where the
information lives — a windowed transform of a one-off random record **biases the peak low**,
because the sharp mode leaks its power into neighbouring bins. The leakage-free multisine, given
**the same plant, the same power, and the same wall-clock**, does not.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Same high-Q mode, same power, same time: leakage-free vs windowed random"
c_leak = md.leakage_campaign(seed=0)
md.leakage_bode_fig(c_leak)
```

The multisine markers sit on the true peak with tight error bars; the windowed-Welch points
read the resonance visibly low. Repeating both over several noise realisations separates the two
failure modes — **bias** (leakage) and **scatter** (variance):

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Peak-bin bias and scatter over several seeds"
v_leak = md.leakage_variance(n_seeds=8)
display(md.leakage_table(v_leak))
```

The random estimator is biased **and** noisier; combined as RMSE at the peak it is many times
worse than the leakage-free multisine carrying identical power for identical time. This is the
single most important reason the package never identifies with random noise: the bias is
systematic, it lands exactly on the high-Q features you care most about, and **averaging longer
does not remove it.**

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## When random noise *is* the right tool
For a **qualitative** whole-band look, a quick **coherence** check, or any broadband floor/
disturbance characterisation where a percent-level peak bias is irrelevant, colored random noise
is fast, simple, and entirely appropriate — and `excitation.timeseries_from_asd` exists for
exactly that. The argument here is against using it as the *quantitative FRF estimator* on a
sharp resonance.
:::

## 4 · The swept sine is slow

The swept sine has no leakage problem and no crest-factor problem — it spends full power on one
clean line at a time. Its cost is **time**: it tours the band **serially**. The multisine measures
**every bin in one window**; in that *same* wall-clock the sweep reaches only a handful of
frequencies (each, fairly, very tight because it spends full power there).

```{python}
#| code-summary: "σ(FRF)/|FRF| — whole-band multisine vs equal-wall-clock swept sine"
c_sweep = md.sweep_campaign(seed=0)
md.sweep_fig(c_sweep)
```

The sweep points sit *on or below* the multisine envelope — full power per line buys low σ at
each visited frequency — but there are only a few of them. **Covering the whole band to the same
per-bin σ costs the sweep the factor annotated on the plot** (here roughly two orders of
magnitude longer than the one multisine window). On a real instrument that is the difference
between a measurement that fits inside a maintenance window and one that does not.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## When the swept sine *is* the right tool
For a **single line** — one calibration tone, one resonance you want pinned to high SNR, a
quick spot check — the swept sine is the obvious choice: nothing beats putting all your power on
the one frequency you care about. It is also the most transparent thing to interpret. The
multisine wins when you need **the whole band**.
:::

## 5 · Optimal excitation wins on time *and* on in-band drive (the headline)

So far the multisine has matched the alternatives where they are weak. The headline result is
where it is *strong*: spend the drive budget not flat across the band, but **concentrated where
the Fisher information is**. `design.pintelon.optimal_excitation` solves for that allocation by
the dispersion-function fixed point (see [Fisher & excitation](fisher.qmd)).

```{python}
#| code-summary: "The optimal drive concentrates power at the modes; CRB variance-reduction F"
head = md.headline_campaign()
md.headline_design_fig(head)
```

The gold drive piles power onto the two resonances instead of spreading it flat. The exact
**Cramér–Rao variance-reduction factor** `F` — worst-parameter, at equal power and time, from
`fisher.parameter_covariance` — is annotated on the design panel. That factor is the budget the
optimal design has to spend, and it can be cashed out **two** ways:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Three real campaigns: flat, optimal (same power), optimal (matched σ)"
md.headline_convergence_fig(head)
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Head-to-head: σ reached, and the drive it took"
display(md.headline_table(head))
```

Read the table honestly, both rows of the optimal arm:

- **At equal drive power**, the optimal multisine reaches a parameter uncertainty several times
  lower than the flat drive in the same number of passes — the flat drive never even crosses the
  σ/θ target inside the budget, while the optimal drive crosses it in a couple of passes. *That
  is the time win,* and it is frame-robust: it is a statement about Fisher information per second,
  independent of any actuator unit.
- **Dialled down to power P/F**, the optimal multisine instead *matches* the flat drive's σ —
  but now at a fraction of the **in-band drive power** (RMS). *That is the drive win:* the same
  answer for materially less in-band power asked of the actuator.

The RMS figures are **plant-referred**. We make **no peak- or crest-drive claim**: concentrating
power does raise the plant-referred crest, but as §2.1 showed, plant-referred crest does not
transfer to the DAC — the limit that actually binds — through the (unmodeled) whitening chain. The
load-bearing wins here are the **time** (whole-band simultaneity) and the **CRB allocation** of
in-band power, both frame-robust.

You do not get both at once for free — `F` is one budget — but you get to **choose** which
scarce resource (time or in-band drive power) to spend it on. Flat excitation gives you neither
choice.

## 6 · A closed loop is not an obstacle

Most LIGO plants are measured **inside a control loop** — the very damping or servo that keeps
the instrument usable suppresses the response you want to see. The naive FRF taken against the
*injected reference* then returns the **suppressed closed-loop response**, not the plant. The
P&S **reference-based** estimate — the ratio of period-averaged spectra against the **drive
monitor** (the true plant input) — cancels the controller and returns the **open-loop plant**,
with no controller model.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "A high-Q mode under a velocity damper: recover the open-loop plant through the live loop"
cl = md.closed_loop_campaign(seed=0)
md.closed_loop_fig(cl)
```

The loop suppresses the resonance by the factor in the title, and the naive estimate dutifully
returns that suppressed curve. The reference-based estimate, against the same data, lands back on
the **open-loop** plant to a fraction of a percent — the controller is *cancelled, not fit*. This
is why "the plant is in a loop" is not a reason to reach for special-case tooling: the same
multisine pipeline handles it. (The DARM page, [example 08](../examples/08-darm-calibration.qmd),
is the same idea on the gravitational-wave readout; the suspension closed loop here is the
general statement.)

## 7 · The consolidated head-to-head

One table, four excitations, the five figures of merit — populated from the real campaigns above
on the representative suspension plants of this page.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Everything, side by side (real numbers from the campaigns)"
display(md.headtohead_table(head, v_leak, c_sweep, cl))
```

The pattern: the swept sine is safe and exact but slow; broadband random is fast but biased on
the high-Q peaks and unsafe to use as the quantitative estimator in a loop; the flat multisine
fixes leakage and the loop but spends its budget indiscriminately; the **optimal multisine**
keeps every multisine advantage and additionally converts the Fisher structure of the plant into
**less time or less drive, your choice.**

## 8 · How any subsystem uses the package

The pipeline is plant-agnostic. To identify a new subsystem you supply two things — a **channel
backend** (how to inject and read) and a **prior model** — and run the loop:

```python
from system_ident.backends.base import ChannelBackend   # implement inject()/read()/ramp_down()
from system_ident.backends.twin import TwinBackend       # or the provided twin/CDS/DARM backends
from system_ident.model import TFModel
from system_ident.loop import SysIDLoop
from system_ident.design.pintelon import PintelonSchoukensDesigner
from system_ident.estimators.gml import GMLEstimator
from system_ident.safety import Watchdog, SafetyLimits

# 1. a prior — even a rough one; the first pass is prior-robust over f0·(1±u)
prior = {"POS": TFModel.from_resonances([(1.0, 50.0)], gain=300.0)}

# 2. a backend that speaks your channels (twin shown; swap in your CDS/hardware backend)
backend = TwinBackend(plant, {"EXC": "POS"}, {"RSP": "POS"},
                      drive_channels={"DRV": "POS"})   # DRV = the loop's drive monitor

# 3. the loop wires designer + estimator + watchdog and runs:
#    measure noise → design optimal multisine → inject (default phase=Schroeder, a
#    free choice that does not affect the FRF; Tukey-ramped for a safe start)
#    → leakage-free reference FRF → ML fit → CRB → redesign → repeat
loop = SysIDLoop(backend, GMLEstimator(), PintelonSchoukensDesigner(),
                 Watchdog(SafetyLimits.from_config(config)))
result = loop.run(config, prior, seed=0)               # result.models["POS"] is the fit
```

Everything on this page is that loop with a different `config` and `prior`. The worked
[examples 01–08](../examples/index.qmd) walk the same path from a single resonance through a
coupled 2×2 suspension, the compiled CDS twin, and the DARM readout — each running the *identical*
diagnostic set (excitation design → time series → magnitude/phase/coherence Bode → residuals →
Cramér–Rao recovery → drive safety → convergence).

## 9 · Honest caveats — and when each alternative is right

No method is free. The optimal multisine carries real assumptions and failure modes, and the
alternatives are genuinely better in specific regimes.

**What the optimal multisine needs.**

- **Synchronous, integer-period capture.** The leakage-free guarantee holds only if the drive is
  periodic over the analysis window and the acquisition is sample-synchronous. Lose period
  alignment (clock drift, dropped samples, a non-integer window) and the leakage advantage
  decays toward the windowed-random case. On CDS this is a wiring requirement, not a given.
- **A prior.** The optimal design is only as good as the model it is computed from. The package
  mitigates this with a **prior-robust first pass** (power spread over `f0·(1±u)`), but a wildly
  wrong prior, an over-specified model order, or a missing mode can misallocate the budget. The
  honest mode of operation is *iterative*: a broad pass, then concentrate.
- **A stationary, linear plant over the window.** The whole-band-in-one-window advantage assumes
  the plant does not drift mid-measurement and responds linearly to the drive. Strong
  nonlinearity or fast non-stationarity breaks the model the CRB is computed against.
- **In a comb-sensitive band, a comb is a cost.** A multisine puts many lines in band at once.
  Where those lines contaminate a science band (e.g. DARM during observation), that footprint is
  a real operational price the swept sine's single line largely avoids — run in non-observing
  time, or use known phases so the lines subtract.
- **The binding actuator limit is at the DAC, and this sim is plant-referred.** In LIGO the hard
  saturation limit is at the **DAC** (counts/volts), with **whitening and actuation filters
  between the digital excitation request and the DAC**. Crest factor is not invariant under
  filtering, so a waveform optimised for low crest in plant/force units (Schroeder phasing,
  concentrated power) is reshaped by the whitening chain and can present an unrelated — generally
  higher — peak at the DAC. This demonstration models only the plant-referred frame and omits
  that chain, so **it makes no crest-factor or peak-drive claim**; the in-band-power (RMS) numbers
  it reports are plant-referred. A genuine peak/crest optimisation is a **DAC-frame, filter-aware**
  problem — push the design through the whitening/actuation model and minimise the peak *there*.
  That is real future work, not something these plant-referred numbers can stand in for.

**When to pick the alternative instead.**

- **Swept sine** — a single line to high SNR, a quick spot check, or any time transparency and
  putting all power on one frequency matter more than band coverage.
- **Broadband random** — a fast qualitative whole-band picture, coherence diagnostics, or
  disturbance/floor characterisation where a percent-level peak bias is irrelevant.
- **Flat multisine** — when you have *no* usable prior at all and want leakage-free, self-error-
  barred whole-band coverage before you know where to concentrate. (It is the package's own first
  pass.)

The optimal multisine is the right default when **all** of: time is scarce, drive is bounded, the
plant is high-Q, the loop is closed, and you have at least a rough prior — which is to say, most
of the time, on most LIGO subsystems. But the package implements **one** pipeline, and the honest
position is to know which knob (and which excitation) the situation calls for.

## References

Pintelon & Schoukens, *System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach*, 2nd ed.,
Wiley-IEEE Press, 2012 — periodic / leakage-free measurement; multisine design and Schroeder
phases (§4); dispersion-function optimal input design (§5.4.2); the reference-based (closed-loop)
FRF; and the Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimator with its Cramér–Rao efficiency.

[LIGO-G2101503](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G2101503) — Fisher-information expressions for
suspension parameters (the form carried by `fisher.fisher_matrix`).

[LIGO-G1400084](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G1400084) (Larry Price) — original motivation and prior
work. See also `notes/darm-calibration-via-pns.md` for the DARM-specific head-to-head and its
literature trail.
